extracted.intended_audience: scientists, academic administrators, university teachers, and scholarly readers of Nature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for (a) university organisation and the appropriateness of specialisation/coordination among universities, and (b) scholarly standards used in reviewing academic monographs in linguistics and chemistry/medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of specialisation in universities
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialisation is appropriate where demand for trained personnel in a particular field is limited and the cost of establishing and maintaining provision in every university would be wasteful; regional accessibility and the 'regional pull' should guide where to concentrate expensive, highly specialised work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: Leeds agreed that new glass-technology work be centred in Sheffield because the Yorkshire glass industry was more accessible from there. The method of settling such cases by conference/co-ordination is recommended to avoid ineffective competition and disappointment when demand is small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of unnecessary overlapping — but allowance for research-related overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: While unnecessary overlapping of university studies should be avoided—especially in times of financial stringency—overlap that provides opportunities for research and teaching vitality is not necessarily wasteful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Minister of Education advised universities to 'take counsel with one another and husband their resources.' The University Grants Committee's report supports the necessity of leisure and opportunity for research; overlapping that enables research is defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for co-operation and co-ordination among universities
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities should co-operate and coordinate to distribute specialised work suitably, especially where large expense is involved or demand is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conference procedure (consultation among universities) is praised as a method for determining distribution of new departments and avoiding needless duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of fundamental humanistic and scientific studies in every university
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental subjects (classics, English, history, mathematics, physics, chemistry, etc.) should be taught in all universities and not be concentrated or specialised away, since such concentration would be harmful to teaching and to the spirit of the university.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialising research in these fundamentals is considered 'a most dangerous principle' and 'contrary to the true spirit of the university'; research opportunities in fundamental subjects should be available broadly to sustain teaching quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of research opportunities for university teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient leisure and facilities to pursue research are essential for university teachers to maintain freshness, mastery, and inspiration in teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted University Grants Committee: 'sufficient leisure to pursue research is as essential as adequate remuneration.' Junior teachers must have research opportunities to rise in their profession and to teach efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/regional subjects should be taught locally where necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects with a regional or local character (e.g., economics involving local investigations, agriculture, forestry, regional languages) should be taught at the local university since travel is inconvenient/expensive and local investigations may be indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative of bringing in visiting teachers may work sometimes but is 'not always possible or desirable' where local investigations are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness and organization for comparative linguistic works (indexing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative linguistic monographs should include clear organization aids such as alphabetical indexes of languages and helpful tables to facilitate research and cross-referencing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes that an 'alphabetical index of languages' would greatly facilitate research and that readers without 'remarkable memory for numbers' are helped by summary tables; lack of such aids forces tedious page-turning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate classification and clear distinction between languages/dialects
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should carefully distinguish distinct languages from dialects and avoid conflating separate languages (e.g., Lala vs Lamba; Chopi vs Tswa vs Lenge vs Hlengwe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer points out specific misclassifications in the book and notes that some errors stem from reliance on limited authorities available when vocabularies were prepared; corrections are possible as new sources become available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical support and primary-source checking for phonetic/usage claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about phonetic phenomena or neologism patterns should be checked against primary sources and native usage (e.g., dictionaries, native newspapers) rather than asserted without verifiable evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer tested the claim about increasing use of clicks by consulting Colenso's Dictionary and a native newspaper ('Ilanga las' e Natal') and reports quantitative findings contrary to the author's broad assertion; emphasizes difficulty of checking without contact with natives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in phonetic analysis and symbol use
rubrics_metrics.description: Phonetic discussions must use precise terminology and symbolization, clearly distinguish different sounds covered by a symbol (e.g., palatal plosive vs palatal-sibilant), and differentiate sentence intonation from word-intonation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer criticizes the book for treating symbols (like ¢, j) as covering multiple sounds without distinction and for failing to clarify differences between sentence-intonation and significant word-intonation; suggests phonetician-level meticulous accuracy is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious historical reconstruction and accurate choice of descriptive terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When restoring hypothetical historical sounds or roots, authors should avoid vague or obsolete labels (e.g., 'guttural') and be cautious in positing specific consonants when evidence is ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes Meinhof's practice of sometimes postulating different consonants (e.g., v) or leaving stems open; criticizes use of 'guttural' as now disused and insufficiently precise, and questions blanket restorations (g vs y, k vs x) without full evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical and evidence-based morphological class assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of noun classes/prefixes should follow logical grouping supported by comparative evidence (e.g., whether diminutive fi- should be placed under class 8 (v-) rather than treated as a separate 8a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer discusses specific proposals (identifying fi- with 8th, treating ka- as a different honorific class) and points to examples from languages (Karanga, Luganda, Konda, Lamba) to illustrate how class functions and historical developments should guide classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of extensive collating and inclusion of under-studied language groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehensive collating, cross-indexing of word-roots, and inclusion of Semi-Bantu and newly identified languages are major scholarly virtues that make a work a standard reference for years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer praises the labour in collating and cross-indexing and highlights the value of examination of Semi-Bantu forms and discovery of previously unsuspected languages (Homa, Bangminda) for shedding light on difficult questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and completeness of laboratory preparative directions in chemical monographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Works describing preparation of organic medicaments should give exact directions for all stages of synthesis, including yields that can be replicated, enabling students to acquire practical manipulative skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer states that detailed preparative directions for substances like phenacetine, stovaine, veronal and salvarsan constitute an important part of the book and give laboratory experience comparable to standard practical manuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between theoretical discussion and practical procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable technical-chemical monograph should combine precise practical methods with theoretical discussion (costs of production, pharmacological testing methods, guiding considerations for drug discovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer praises Fourneau's theoretical section (cost considerations, pharmacological testing, searching for new anaesthetics) in addition to the practical recipes, noting both parts are excellent and complementary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice on apparatus set-up and laboratory practice (aesthetics and care)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance to beginners should include careful, neat apparatus assembly and laboratory discipline—an aesthetic ideal for apparatus set-up that promotes safety and good technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted advice: 'The laboratory should be kept like a drawing-room' and Moissan's ideal that the chemist 'should be able to work

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical and chemical accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical books should minimize typographical and chemical-structural errors; errata may rectify some mistakes but core chemical formulae should be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes several misspellings of names and some chemical formula errors (quinine, trypaflavine) remaining despite an errata list; these are considered minor blemishes but worth mentioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of work for intended audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and reviewers should consider which readership the book best serves (e.g., advanced students, pharmacologists, technical chemists) and recommend accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer recommends Fourneau's book to advanced students and pharmacologists as a source of information, and notes that recommending it to technical chemists (former director of industrial labs) is unnecessary.
